title: Prepare a lesson
lead: You want your class to be more participatory.
question: What is the biggest challenge in your next lesson?

options.label: Teach fractions in an engaging way
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. I need to teach fractions to fifth graders and I want my students to participate more. What would you suggest?
options.gabi: Hi! We could start with something concrete: represent fractions using paper strips or drawings. Then each group explains how they found their answer. What would you like to focus on?

follow.label: A quick activity to get started
follow.user: A short activity to start the lesson would help.
follow.gabi: You could hand out paper and ask students to make one half, one third and one quarter. Have them compare results in pairs before sharing with the class.
follow.take: Useful guidance starts with describing the class, the content and what you want to achieve.

follow.label: A way to check understanding
follow.user: I would like to know how to check that they understood fractions.
follow.gabi: At the end, show two shapes and ask students to explain which one represents the given fraction and why. Their explanations can help you identify questions.
follow.take: AI can suggest strategies, but the teacher interprets students’ responses.

options.label: Include students who rarely speak
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. Some students in my class hardly ever participate. How can I give them more opportunities?
options.gabi: You could try written responses first, then conversations in pairs, before inviting contributions in front of the whole group. What would you like to explore?

follow.label: Working in pairs
follow.user: I would like to try an activity in pairs.
follow.gabi: Ask a short question, allow one minute to think and then two minutes to discuss in pairs. Afterwards, invite students to share ideas without making anyone present.
follow.take: Suggested strategies should always be adapted to the group and its needs.

follow.label: Participating without public speaking
follow.user: Are there ways to participate without everyone having to speak in front of the class?
follow.gabi: Yes. You could use anonymous notes, coloured cards or individual responses that are discussed together.
follow.take: Profe Gabi’s guidance complements the teacher’s judgment and observation.

options.label: Plan a simple assessment
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. I want to prepare a simple assessment to understand what my class has learned.
options.gabi: You could start by defining the learning you need to observe. Then choose a short piece of evidence, such as an explanation, an example or an exercise. What would help most?

follow.label: An end-of-lesson question
follow.user: I need a question to close the lesson.
follow.gabi: Try: “What did you learn today, and what example would you use to explain it to someone else?” Adapt the question to your lesson objective.
follow.take: The tool supports planning; it does not replace the teacher’s assessment decisions.

follow.label: Assess without a long test
follow.user: I would rather assess learning without a lengthy test.
follow.gabi: You could use a two-question exit ticket or ask for a short explanation. Review the answers and decide what to revisit in the next lesson.
follow.take: The aim is to support specific, practical teaching decisions.

title: Manage my class
lead: Your group talks a lot and struggles to stay focused.
question: Which situation would you like to address?

options.label: Too much noise and distraction
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. My seventh-grade class talks a lot and I lose time trying to regain their attention.
options.gabi: I understand. You could establish a clear starting signal, suggest short tasks and agree on participation rules with the group. Where would you like to begin?

follow.label: Create classroom agreements
follow.user: I want to develop agreements with the class.
follow.gabi: Invite students to suggest two or three actions that help everyone listen and participate. Display them somewhere visible and review them together regularly.
follow.take: AI suggests ways to improve the classroom environment; the teacher decides and supports the group.

follow.label: Regain attention without shouting
follow.user: How can I respectfully regain their attention?
follow.gabi: Try a short, consistent signal, wait a few seconds and resume with a clear instruction. Observe what works best in your context.
follow.take: Support can help you consider practical options without imposing decisions.

options.label: Improve teamwork
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. When my students work in teams, some do everything while others do not get involved.
options.gabi: You could assign rotating roles and a very specific goal to each team. Would you like to start with roles or with assessing the teamwork?

follow.label: Define roles for everyone
follow.user: It would help to define roles within the team.
follow.gabi: You could rotate who coordinates, takes notes, presents and checks that everyone has contributed. Change roles for each activity.
follow.take: Suggestions are starting points for designing a better classroom experience.

follow.label: Check that everyone contributes
follow.user: I want to know whether each team member contributed.
follow.gabi: At the end, ask for a short individual reflection: what I contributed, what I learned and what support I needed. Compare these responses with your observations.
follow.take: Professional judgment remains with the teacher.

options.label: Handle an argument during class
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. Two students argued in the middle of a lesson. I want to respond without making the conflict worse.
options.gabi: You can separate the immediate situation from a later conversation: first restore calm and safety, then listen to those involved according to your school’s procedures. What do you need?

follow.label: Reduce tension in the moment
follow.user: I need a way to reduce tension in that moment.
follow.gabi: Speak calmly, avoid singling students out in front of the group and ask the school team for support if the situation calls for it.
follow.take: In complex conflicts, the tool does not replace procedures or human support.

follow.label: Talk after the incident
follow.user: I would like to know how to talk afterwards.
follow.gabi: You could ask what happened, how they felt and what actions might help repair the situation, following your school’s guidance.
follow.take: Human support and school procedures remain essential.

title: Care for my wellbeing
lead: You feel your teaching workload building up each week.
question: What would you like to talk about?

options.label: I cannot prepare everything in time
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. I am an early-career teacher and I feel I do not have enough time to plan my lessons.
options.gabi: That can happen when you are starting out. You could organise tasks by urgency and importance, and reuse lesson planning structures. What would you like to organise first?

follow.label: Prioritise my tasks
follow.user: I want to learn how to prioritise what I need to do.
follow.gabi: Write down what you need to resolve tomorrow, what you can plan this week and what you should discuss with your team. Start with one important, manageable task.
follow.take: Profe Gabi can support work organisation, but cannot take on every responsibility.

follow.label: Simplify lesson planning
follow.user: I need to plan without starting from scratch every time.
follow.gabi: You could create a simple template with an objective, an opening activity, practice and a closing activity. Adapt it to each group and ask colleagues what materials already exist.
follow.take: Guidance helps identify practical steps and seek support from the school team.

options.label: I take work home
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. I am taking a lot of schoolwork home and I want to organise myself better.
options.gabi: We can think about small, realistic strategies. Would you rather review your schedule or look for support to share tasks?

follow.label: Organise my schedule
follow.user: I would like to review how I use my time.
follow.gabi: Try setting aside short blocks for planning and marking, along with defined breaks. Afterwards, review what was realistic to maintain.
follow.take: Teacher wellbeing also depends on working conditions and institutional support.

follow.label: Ask my team for support
follow.user: I want to talk with colleagues so I do not have to do everything alone.
follow.gabi: You could explain which tasks take the most time and ask about shared materials or ways to prioritise. You do not need to solve everything on your own.
follow.take: The tool complements, but does not replace, a human support network.

options.label: I feel uncertain as I start teaching
options.user: Hi, Profe Gabi. I am starting to teach and sometimes I really doubt my decisions.
options.gabi: Learning to teach takes time. It can help to identify a specific situation, recognise what worked and talk with a mentor about what you would improve. What would be most useful?

follow.label: Reflect after a lesson
follow.user: I want to learn how to reflect on how my lesson went.
follow.gabi: You could write down three things: what you wanted to achieve, what you observed and what you would change. Choose just one adjustment for next time.
follow.take: Support combines professional reflection with human guidance.

follow.label: Prepare to talk with my mentor
follow.user: I want to know how to ask my mentor for guidance.
follow.gabi: Bring a specific example from your class, explain what you tried and ask a clear question. This can help focus the conversation on ways to improve.
follow.take: Profe Gabi aims to complement mentoring, not replace it.
